e7a2f12a626c10b2: Hull hold Chelsea, Liverpool fail to beat Fulham in Premier League
AFP
LONDON: Hull held free-scoring Chelsea 2-2 at Stamford Bridge to go third in the Premier League as Liverpool failed to find a way past struggling Fulham in a 0-0 draw on Saturday.
It was a familiar tale for Chelsea as the front three of Morgan Rogers, Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer dazzled, but the Blues were undone by an inability to defend.
In five games against top-flight opposition since Xabi Alonso took charge, Chelsea have scored 16 times and conceded 12.
Hull were the last side in the Premier League to concede, but after three clean sheets they were finally breached when Rogers drilled in at the near post on seven minutes.
Mohamed Belloumi took advantage of Chelsea's slackness at the back to blast home on the volley after Jorrel Hato got caught under a cross to the back post.
The Algerian winger then put Hull in front with a deflected strike after Emi Martinez failed to deal with a corner.
Pedro drilled a Palmer cross into the top corner to bring Chelsea level just after the hour mark.
But the home side could not find a winner as Hull's honeymoon back in the Premier League goes on with only defending champions Arsenal and Manchester City above them in the table.
- FULHAM FIGHT FOR ARBELOA -
Liverpool remain unbeaten under Andoni Iraola but there were boos at Anfield after Fulham picked up their first point under Alvaro Arbeloa.
Former Liverpool defender Arbeloa was reportedly fighting for his job after losing his first three league matches since arriving in west London from Real Madrid.
Yet a Liverpool forward line featuring three £100 million (US$135 million) players in Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak failed to click against the Cottagers' leaky defence.

Indeed it was Fulham who had the better chances to take all three points as Gonzalo Garcia missed a glorious opportunity in the first half and Alisson Becker produced a brilliant save to deny Josh King the winner.
Liverpool climb to sixth but could find themselves already six points off the top should Arsenal win at Sunderland later on Saturday.
Aston Villa are rooted in the relegation zone after Nottingham Forest exacted revenge with a 2-1 win at Villa Park.
Villa beat their Midlands rivals in the Europa League semi-finals last season on their way to lifting a first trophy for 30 years.
Many eyebrows were raised at the club record reported £45 million Forest paid Chelsea for Liam Delap after failing to make the grade at Stamford Bridge.
But Delap proved his worth with a long-range strike into the bottom corner to open the scoring.
Alysson levelled with Villa's first league goal of the season, but Igor Jesus secured Oliver Glasner's first win as Forest boss.
Glasner's old club Crystal Palace's poor start to the campaign continued with a 3-2 home defeat to Ipswich.
The visitors were aided by Axel Disasi's first half red card as Zian Flemming's first goal for the Tractor Boys snatched all three points in stoppage time.
Brentford remain unbeaten thanks to Kevin Schade's double in a 2-2 draw at Bournemouth.
The Cherries, by contrast, are yet to win in the Premier League under Marco Rose despite leading in all four games.
Tottenham are aiming to kickstart their league season with a first goal and win at home to Everton later.
Manchester United host local rivals City in the pick of Sunday's action.

71c46e887c13c496: KUALA LUMPUR: Former High Court judge Datuk Syed Ahmad Idid Syed Abdullah Idid has clarified that he never requested, demanded, or set a compensation amount of RM10.5 million from the Malaysian government over his resignation nearly 30 years ago.
He clarified to clear up confusion regarding the reported claim through a letter sent today to Malaysian Bar president Anand Raj.

Syed Ahmad Idid also expressed his deep appreciation to the Malaysian Bar for its firm stance in defending the independence and integrity of the judiciary through its statement issued yesterday, titled "The Judiciary Must Be, and Remain, Steadfast in Upholding the Rule of Law and Incorruptible".
He explained that the RM10.5 million figure linked to him in recent reports actually referred to other judges affected by the 1988 judicial crisis.
"Those circumstances were materially different from my case. Therefore, I consider it inappropriate for my case to be equated with theirs based on that figure," he said.
"On my part, I have never requested, demanded, or specified an amount of RM10.5 million, nor have I suggested any specific sum as compensation from the government," he added.

Elaborating further, he emphasised that his resignation was not merely a personal matter involving pensions or financial compensation, but a fundamental question of legal and constitutional principles regarding how a High Court judge resigns.

"My intention and priority have always transcended personal interest. An independent judiciary relies on judges who can execute their constitutional duties with complete integrity without fear or favour," he said.
"Anyone who raises truth-based concerns regarding misconduct within our institutions should not be punished, but protected," he added.
He expressed hope that his experiences three decades ago would help strengthen the judicial institution for future generations.

Syed Ahmad Idid resigned as a High Court judge in 1996 after exposing alleged misconduct and corruption within the judiciary through an anonymous letter containing 112 allegations against certain judges at the time.

d92438f95c3adb58: NEW DELHI: BRICS has called for the immediate restoration of an accessible, effective, and fully functioning two-tier binding World Trade Organisation (WTO) dispute settlement mechanism while reaffirming its support for a rules-based multilateral trading system.

"We remain committed to active engagement in multilateral negotiations in Geneva, especially in the debates regarding the reform of the WTO," the grouping said in a 45-page declaration released today.
BRICS said it would enhance coordination under its Informal Consultative Framework to address challenges undermining the WTO's effectiveness and credibility.

The grouping also called for the appointment of new Appellate Body members without delay, stressing the importance of strengthening the organisation's authority, effectiveness, inclusiveness, and relevance.

"We strongly advocate for the immediate restoration of an accessible, effective, fully functioning, two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism as a foundation for trust and predictability for all WTO members, and the appointment of new Appellate Body members without further delay," the declaration stated.

The grouping expressed serious concern over the proliferation of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures inconsistent with WTO rules, warning that such actions threaten to reduce global trade, disrupt supply chains, and deepen economic disparities. It also condemned unilateral coercive measures contrary to international law, including economic and secondary sanctions not authorised by the United Nations Security Council.

Furthermore, BRICS encouraged the New Development Bank (NDB) to expand its capacity to mobilise resources, foster innovation, expand local currency financing, diversify funding sources, and support impactful projects advancing sustainable development.
"We recognise NDB as a crucial BRICS institution for promoting sustainable development, reducing inequalities and supporting resilience in emerging economies," it said.

Echoing the aspirations of the Global South to integrate into the multilateral trading system, BRICS supported Ethiopia and Iran's bids to join the WTO, while acknowledging China's expansion of zero-tariff treatment to 53 African nations with which it maintains diplomatic ties.
China is set to assume the BRICS chairmanship in 2027 and host the 19th BRICS Leaders' Summit.

Initially established by Brazil, Russia, India, and China, the forum expanded to include South Africa in 2011, followed by Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates in 2023, and Indonesia in 2024.
Malaysia, alongside Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Nigeria, Thailand, Vietnam, Uganda, and Uzbekistan, joined as BRICS partner countries.
India, which previously held the chairmanship in 2012, 2016, and 2021, assumed its fourth BRICS chairmanship on Jan 1, 2026, marking 20 years since the grouping's establishment.

f584880c9d6e2b35: IPOH: Dr L Sivanaesan has been appointed the new president of the Malaysian Medical Association (MMA), succeeding Datuk Dr R Thirunavukarasu, whose term ended today.

The former MMA president-elect previously served as chairman of MMA Selangor, honorary deputy secretary of the association for two terms, and chairman of the MMA Private Practitioners Section from 2023 to 2024.

Speaking at the MMA 2026 dinner here tonight, Sivanaesan said retaining doctors in Malaysia's public healthcare system will be his priority as the nation faces growing healthcare demands and an increasing need for medical personnel.

"Training a doctor takes many years and requires significant investment," he said. "When experienced doctors leave the public system, we do not simply lose a member of the workforce; we lose experience, expertise and the continuity of care they provide to patients."

Sivanaesan said retaining doctors cannot be addressed simply by increasing the number of medical graduates, noting that greater attention must be given to doctors' career progression, working environment, professional development and long-term prospects within the public healthcare system.

822c243ee6644e58: JOHOR BARU: Police have arrested a 25-year-old local man suspected of robbing, assaulting, and threatening two Rohingya men in Taman Perling.
Johor police chief Datuk Ab Rahaman Arsad said police received reports regarding the incidents on Sept 9 and 10 from the victims, aged 25 and 35.
"The first victim was riding a motorcycle looking for lawn-mowing clients when the suspect stopped him, demanding and snatching his UNHCR card and lawnmower.
"The suspect then confronted the second victim nearby, demanding his UNHCR card before punching and threatening him during an altercation," Ab Rahaman said in a statement today.
Following a tip-off, a team from the Johor Baru Utara district police headquarters criminal investigation department arrested the suspect in Taman Perling at 5.40pm yesterday.
Ab Rahaman said police seized a lawnmower, a parang, a UNHCR card, a motorcycle key, and a set of clothes.
The suspect, who tested negative for drugs but has a prior criminal record, has been remanded for seven days until Sept 18 to assist investigations.

"Police are verifying the authenticity of the victims' UNHCR cards with the UNHCR Office in Kuala Lumpur. At the same time, we stress that any party other than the authorities who detains, blocks, or checks an individual's identification documents is acting against the law," he said.
The case is being investigated under Section 392 of the Penal Code for robbery, Section 323 for voluntarily causing hurt, and Section 506 for criminal intimidation.

63629f68c88d9788: PETALING JAYA: Social media has overtaken television and news websites as Malaysians' most widely used news source, according to the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism.

The institute's 2026 Digital News Report showed that print media had collapsed from 45% in 2017 to 14% in 2026. Television has also declined, from 54% to 36% over the same period while online and social media sites have risen steadily since 2024.
The report also noted that 69% of respondents used social media for news in 2026, compared with 42% for news websites and 36% for television.

Around a third (32%) of Malaysians now access content from influencers and content creators who are focussed on the news. Major influencers seen as being popular included former Umno Youth chief Khairy Jamaluddin (Keluar Sekejap podcast) and retired politician and technocrat Idris Jala (The Game of Impossible podcast).

The report highlighted that WhatsApp remained the most popularly used social media platform for news sources at 58%, followed by Facebook (49%), TikTok (45%), YouTube (41%), Instagram (24%) and Telegram (16%).
Meanwhile, trust in news media stood at 40% in 2023 after it peaked at 41% in 2021, which the Reuters Institute said reflects optimism around a new reformist government.

Trust level stabilised at 37% for two consecutive years, but dropped significantly to 30% this year, which the report said indicates waning optimism. Overall trust in the news rose to 30% in 2026, up a point from 29% in 2017. The report said Malaysia's trust rate is seven points below the global average of 37%.

14908610fcda4e49: NEW YORK: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday called on artificial intelligence (AI) firms to slow down the development of the powerful technology, amid mounting worries over the risks of "superintelligent" computer systems.

His comments came a few days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement.

"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," Amodei wrote in a post on his personal website.
"AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious."

"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way," said Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela in 2021.
"But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence."
Amodei's statement echoes another call by Anthropic in early June to slow or suspend development.
Then in late July, Sam Altman, the boss of Anthropic rival OpenAI, said developers might need to voluntarily pump the brakes on their rapid advances to give society a chance to catch up.

At roughly the same time, more than 1,000 employees at cutting-edge AI companies including Amodei signed a petition calling on the US government to help "deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development."
OpenAI had revealed that during testing, the AI models broke out of their confined environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site developers use to store and share code.

Earlier this week, Coxon, 27, sounded the alarm after spending the past three years pretraining AI models - first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach.
Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data.
"Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Coxon said Tuesday.
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," he said in a post on X.
Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI's capabilities exceed human intelligence.

323f6024bcc6bc85: STARK warnings from artificial intelligence researchers that advanced forms of the technology could wipe out humanity have raised questions over whether governments are moving fast enough to regulate it.
What are the potential dangers of "superintelligent" computer systems, and should we be worried?
AI experts have long described the threat as critical.

In 2023, hundreds of AI scientists and industry figures, including the heads of top US labs, signed a "statement on AI extinction risk" calling for the issue to be treated as seriously as pandemics or nuclear war.

If an out-of-control future AI deems that humans are obstructing its goals, it could use robots to "synthesise and spread novel pathogens", said Stuart Russell, computer science professor at the University of California, Berkeley.
Or it could "convince people to initiate nuclear war, including by hacking into early warning systems", Russell, a prominent voice on AI safety, said.

Such existential fears do not concern current AI systems, he said. But as the technology improves, it could take lethal action beyond our understanding, such as by removing oxygen from the atmosphere.
"We are less intelligent than superintelligent AI. If you ask chimpanzees how humans could wipe them out, they probably wouldn't be able to give you all the right answers."
In the meantime, "in the next year or two, I think the risk is higher from human misuse", Russell added, such as an AI-enabled terror attack.
"The stakes are well-understood," Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher, wrote on X last week, announcing his resignation from US AI startup Anthropic.
"But they are locked in a race to get there first," he added, saying that Anthropic "believes no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves".
Anthropic this year removed a pledge from its safety charter to halt development of its models if it failed to control their risks.
It argued that if it unilaterally paused its work, its less cautious rivals would dominate the industry, making it less safe overall.
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," said Coxon, who previously worked at ChatGPT maker Open-AI.
He accused both companies of "gambling with our lives" as they strive to develop AI models capable of self-improvement.
Fears are heightened over rogue AI after OpenAI technology operating outside human supervision hacked into Hugging Face, a repository of AI models.
"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" Anthropic safety executive Evan Hubinger chimed in on X, estimating the risk at more than 10 per cent over the next decade.
It's important to remember that doom-laden percentage predictions are "absolutely unscientific", said Hussein Abbass, a computing professor at UNSW Canberra.
"The situation is still controllable, and it can be managed," Abbass said.
But governments should not sit on their hands when it comes to regulating AI, he added, urging an "agile" approach as AI development accelerates.
Both Anthropic and OpenAI are expected to go public soon, and some sceptics say scary warnings make AI appear powerful and worthy of large investments.
Others argue that focusing on the risk of extinction distracts from more pressing problems caused by AI, from job losses to machines discriminating against minorities.
In July, more than 1,000 tech employees, including Anthropic's CEO, called on Washington to support a coordinated slowdown in the development of the most advanced AI systems.
OpenAI halted training of its latest models for two weeks in August before resuming it under tighter controls.
The United States has been firmly against global regulation of the sector that could stifle innovation.
But the hacking capabilities of the most cutting-edge models have given Washington pause, with recent Anthropic and OpenAI releases delayed over national security concerns.
Even then, "we don't want to restrict them where all of a sudden we come in second to China", President Donald Trump has said.

"Maybe it will take a massive, Chernobyl-scale disaster to get governments to act," Russell said, urging them to establish a licensing regime for AI, as exists with aviation, medicine or water supply.
"Perhaps at some point governments will remember that their voters prefer not to be dead."

f699d9b1cbe8fc36: TWENTY-SIX years ago, a journalist with about six years of experience decided he needed to further his studies to get a degree to improve his chances of growing in the industry.
He chose a university well known for its mass communications courses — and one that was affordable — in a Midwestern part of the United States.
The next year, he was appointed news editor of the university's newspaper due in large part to his experience, meagre as it was.
One fateful morning that year, the journalist in question woke up a little late and rushed to get ready, forgoing his usual habit of watching the news on TV.
As he got into the elevator of his dormitory later, he heard some others talking about an aircraft crashing into the Twin Towers in New York.
The journalist thought nothing of it, thinking it was a light aircraft.
He did not realise then the scale of what was happening on Sept 11, 2001.
It was only when he got to his first class of the day — in a remarkable coincidence, it was on terrorism — that he knew exactly what was going on.
A TV had been wheeled into the classroom, and students were watching as things unfolded.
But the students actually knew what was happening before it unfolded on TV.

The lecturer was a retired lieutenant-colonel in the US Air Force who had once been posted at the US embassy in Moscow. She had many friends in the intelligence agencies and stepped out constantly to answer or make phone calls.
She kept her students informed, telling them about the crash into the Pentagon and the fourth aircraft, even before it crashed in Pennsylvania.
We all know the story of what unfolded that day. The chaos, the weeping, the fear, the death, the anger. The first thing that hit everyone, however, was shock and disbelief.
In the university's theatre, which holds about 700 people, more than 1,000 students and lecturers sat and stood in shock, watching a large screen showing a news channel.

Then, as the first tower came crashing down, a collective gasp rocked the theatre. This was followed by the exact opposite — complete and utter silence, a deafening silence broken only by the sounds of sobbing.
The university cancelled classes for the rest of the day and warned foreign students to stay at home.
The journalist received calls from worried friends telling him to stay home and not attend a vigil being planned for that night. He had to ignore their advice, though, as he had a job to do.
That worry came to nothing, as everyone was supportive of foreign students and looked out for them.
The fears were justified, but proved unnecessary. There was only sorrow that lingered.
Twenty-five years on, the journalist still remembers everything that happened that day as if it were a mere 25 minutes ago.
Every thought, every emotion — fear, sadness, anger — still lingers.
Sept 11, 2001, will remain with him all the days of his life. It is there alongside the memories of Malaysia Airlines flights MH370 and MH17.
The people who died that day will remain a part of his memory, despite the fact that he did not know them. But so will all those who showed their concern for him.
It is at our worst times that people come through for us. Let us all, in others' times of need, be there for them.

bf65d7c158441678: THIS marks a positive and long-awaited step towards addressing the imbalance in Malaysia's federal structure and fulfilling the broader spirit of the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63). There is no disagreement here.

Greater representation for Sabah and Sarawak is a positive recognition that Malaysia's federal structure must evolve to reflect the realities and aspirations of all its regions. It is a evolution, not a revolution. But the goal should not be to create winners and losers between East and West Malaysia.
A stronger voice for Sabah and Sarawak should be seen as strengthening the entire federation.

The real test will be whether the increased representation leads to better policies, greater development and a more equitable partnership within Malaysia. This is one more step towards that direction.
Greater representation would recognise the special position of Sabah and Sarawak as partners in the formation of Malaysia. This would signal better representation for remote communities.

Constituencies in Sabah and Sarawak can be geographically vast and difficult to serve. More representatives could help bring Parliament closer to remote communities. It could lead to a more balanced federation: national policies should reflect the needs and perspectives of all regions.
A stronger Borneo voice can enrich national debate and improve policymaking.

However, representation must mean more than numbers. More members of parliament alone will not solve Sabah and Sarawak's long-standing concerns over infrastructure, healthcare, education and development. Greater representation must be accompanied by real progress.
Hectares of forests are gone over the years, yet very little evidence of economic development shows up. Don't get us wrong.
There were, of course, spurts of it in the 1970s, 1980s and more evidently, in the late 2000s. Spurt doesn't do development justice. Developed years, they called them.
There is a peculiar connection between politics and economics. If political leadership is strong, it will drive development like it does now in Sarawak.
One won't be wrong to say that Kuching has seen a sea change in the last decade or two. Likewise, 20 years of commerce is a great persuader too. At times, it is otherwise.

In Sabah, it is quieter. Now, with more Borneo voices in Parliament, Kuala Lumpur gets louder — as long as equity is somewhere there. "No one must be left behind" is a great line, if it just remains a line in a prime minister's keynote address at an international forum.
Yes, equity is the point. In the beginning is the end.

"The idea is to focus on non-ringgit sukuk issuances that translate national priorities into clear, credible and globally recognisable purposes under the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)," he said in his opening remarks.
Mohammad Faiz said the framework would be Shariah-based and aligned with the SC's Maqasid al-Shariah Guidance, while also adopting the Asean Taxonomy and international green bond principles.
He said the proposal was still a work in progress and the SC welcomed feedback from participants at the roundtable.
The initiative comes as Malaysia seeks to scale up financing for climate adaptation and resilience amid increasing losses from extreme weather events.
Mohammad Faiz said Malaysia, located in a climate-vulnerable region, had suffered more than US$2.2 billion (RM8.95 billion) in losses from floods — its main climate risk — over the past five years.
"These temperatures are not simply statistics or mere projections. They signal a change that will have profound implications for infrastructure, investments and our resilience," he said.
He said sustainable and responsible finance would be critical in facilitating the funding needed to help economies adapt to and mitigate the effects of climate change.
However, he said stronger market infrastructure and clearer adaptation-focused frameworks were needed to measure and verify outcomes.
"Without these foundations, scaling private capital towards climate resilience will remain constrained because investors cannot underwrite what they cannot measure," he said.
Mohammad Faiz said Malaysia was not starting from scratch, having built a comprehensive ecosystem for sustainable finance.

He said outstanding SRI sukuk had grown from US$1.3 billion in 2020 to US$12.9 billion last year, while Malaysia ranked among the region's top three issuers of green, social, sustainability and sustainability-linked bonds and sukuk.
This accounted for about a quarter of total regional issuances, he said.

Under the SC's Capital Market Masterplan 2026-2030, Malaysia aims to mobilise about US$24.6 billion over five years towards climate transition, adaptation, resilience and social development initiatives.
Mohammad Faiz said the roundtable would focus on identifying scalable and investable solutions capable of delivering measurable resilience outcomes.
He said this could include outcome-linked and resilience-based sukuk, blended finance and other innovative structures to improve the bankability of adaptation investments.
"Our task over the next two days is to develop workable proposals for the wider world to use within the ambit of financing climate adaptation and resilience and Islamic finance," he said.

47fa6e77a70012dc: LETTERS: Haze is far more than a seasonal nuisance.
Treating it as a temporary inconvenience risks underestimating the harm it can cause.

Behind Air Pollutant Index (API) numbers are real people, including children going to school, workers commuting to the office, elderly people going about daily routines and individuals with respiratory and cardiovascular problems trying to breathe normally.
This is why people are repeatedly advised to reduce outdoor activities when air quality deteriorates.
But there is an uncomfortable question we cannot ignore. Why expose our lungs to cigarette smoke when the air around us is already polluted?
Cigarette smoke contains thousands of chemicals that can damage the lungs and cardiovascular system.
During a haze episode, continuing to smoke adds another source of harmful pollutants to an already compromised respiratory environment.
It is, quite simply, a double burden on the lungs. The danger does not stop with smokers.
Second-hand smoke exposes family members, colleagues and members of the public to harmful substances.
For smokers, the haze should therefore be viewed not only as a reason to stay indoors but also as a reason to quit. This is where public health messaging must become more integrated.
When authorities advise people to monitor API readings, limit outdoor activities and protect vulnerable groups, tobacco control should be part of that conversation.

A haze episode should be treated as a powerful teachable moment. If people are concerned about breathing polluted air from the environment, they should also recognise the additional harm caused by inhaling cigarette smoke.
The responsibility, however, does not rest entirely with individuals. Government agencies, healthcare professionals, employers, schools and universities must get involved.
Breathing polluted air should never become normal. Nor should smoking during the haze be dismissed as an individual's personal choice.
DR MOHD ROZAIMY RIDZUAN Lecturer Faculty of Administrative Science and Policy Studies UiTM Pahang Branch, Raub Campus

e15ee510c15dd525: LONDON: Hundreds of anti-immigration protesters and counter-demonstrators faced off Saturday in the southern English city of Portsmouth, at closely-watched duelling rallies which authorities fear could descend into unrest after violent scenes there last Sunday.

Anti-migrant protesters calling themselves "patriots" and opponents from the Stand Up to Racism group rallied from around noon (1100 GMT), with police announcing a ban on face masks ahead of the gatherings.
Officers kept the two sides apart as they massed on either side of a central square after separate marches through parts of the port city.

It comes after anti-migrant demonstrators - many dressed in black and wearing masks - clashed with police there six days ago after asylum seekers who had crossed the Channel from France in a small boat were landed nearby.
Official vehicles were damaged and a small number of officers were injured, according to police, with the government condemning the scenes as "thuggish".

The day before, hundreds of masked protesters had also massed in Dover, further east, briefly blocking access to the town's busy Channel port to demonstrate against migrant crossings and also drawing criticism from political leaders.
"We're making a stand," retiree Colin O'Malley told AFP as he turned out for Saturday's anti-migrant protest, where attendees waved British union jack and England's national St George's flags.
"We're sending a message to the government... illegal immigration has got out of hand, and it needs to stop," he said.

The arrival each year of tens of thousands of migrants aboard small boats has become highly contentious in Britain, relentlessly seized upon by the hard-right and helping fuel growing anti-immigration sentiment.
Those who showed up at the Stand Up to Racism rally chanted "refugees are welcome here" and other slogans.
Attendee John Woods told AFP they were "showing that the far right do not own this city".
"The vast majority of people are opposed to racism, opposed to far-right thugs marching through our city (and) welcome refugees," he added.
Hampshire Police - responsible for Portsmouth - announced Friday that it was banning masks at Saturday's protests to "reduce opportunities for violence, intimidation and criminality".
It said the move followed "recent incidents of violence and intimidation by a minority of those who have been intent on disrupting peaceful protest".

Leaders from across the political spectrum criticised last weekend's unrest in Portsmouth and Dover, which they blamed on far-right agitators, with interior minister Shabana Mahmood meeting police bosses Thursday to get reassurance they were prepared for further incidents.

95ce3aab2941faf2: MADRID: Championship leader Kimi Antonelli stayed on top for Mercedes ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc in Saturday's extended crash-hit third and final practice ahead of qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old Italian clocked a best lap in one minute and 32.797 seconds to outpace the Monegasque by 0.166 seconds ahead of both McLarens in a session that saw seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton slam into the barriers in the second Ferrari.

Hamilton's crash led to a red flag stoppage that lasted 54 minutes and rendered an extra quarter of an hour added, as the drivers' continued to explore the limits of the new high-risk Madring circuit, dubbed a 'car-killer' in many quarters.

In the end, Antonelli's pure talent took him clear again with Leclerc second ahead of Oscar Piastri and world champion Lando Norris with four-time champion Max Verstappen taking fifth for Red Bull in the final minutes.

George Russell was sixth in the second Mercedes, seven-tenths off his team-mate's pace, ahead of Liam Lawson in the second Red Bull, Nico Hulkenberg of Audi, Hamilton and Gabriel Bortoleto in the second Audi.

After a crash-free opening hour on Friday, the second produced one crash – for Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad, who returned to take 14th place, and the third delivered two as Oliver Bearman also hit the barriers in his Haas in the final minute.
After a slow start, Ferrari had joined the fray on softs and clocked immediate fastest laps before a hasty Hamilton slammed into the barriers.

The 41-year-old Briton locked up at the final corner after 24 minutes, breaking his front wing which was stuck under the car as he reversed successfully and began to return to the pits. The session was red-flagged.

Race engineer Carlo Santi realised and asked him to "stop in the safest place possible" but Hamilton was not keen to obey. He replied, saying "if I can make it back, I will. If not, I will do it safely".

Told he had a right front puncture and told again to stop, he finally pulled up, knowing he had ignored orders, driven in an unsafe condition and probably faced a penalty. It was, he knew, a bad incident for him.
With 15 minutes remaining, Race Control stopped the timer to allow a final quarter of an hour action once repairs were completed.

This was a rare occurrence as F1 does not usually allow for additional time, except for qualifying sessions, but it guaranteed a frantic finale for a sell-out crowd basking in the sun with the young Italian jousting with Leclerc.

476b7f115287a9c0: DUBLIN: Donald Trump said Saturday he would "love to see" a united Ireland, wading into a politically sensitive subject as he embarked on a two-day Irish visit that blurs the lines between his presidency and personal business interests.
After meeting Ireland's prime minister Micheal Martin in Dublin, Trump said reunification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland - split for over a century - would be "a fantastic thing".
"The way I look at it, it's going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now," he told reporters, adding though that "the UK will have something to say about it, obviously".
The island of Ireland has been split between the Irish republic in the south and Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom, since 1921.

Under the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which ended three decades of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland that killed about 3,000 people, a referendum can be held if the UK government determines a majority there is likely to favour joining the Republic of Ireland.
The people of the Republic of Ireland would also have to vote in favour for reunification to occur.
The United States has previously adopted a position of neutrality on the issue.
UK prime minister Andy Burnham insisted last month that a unity referendum was "off the table", drawing a sharp response from the pro-unity party Sinn Fein.

Asked about Trump's comments, a spokesperson for his Downing Street office referred reporters to comments Burnham made in parliament Wednesday when he vowed to "stick to the Good Friday Agreement 100%".
Divergences
However Gavin Robinson, leader of the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said on X that "as unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic".
The US president had touched down at Dublin airport shortly before 8.25am (0725 GMT) under a security operation dubbed one of the largest ever mounted in Ireland.

At least 4,000 police and other personnel, including snipers, are mobilised for the visit, which will see Trump fly to his luxury resort in Doonbeg on Ireland's west coast to watch the Irish Open golf tournament.
He inspected a military guard of honour after being received by left-wing president Catherine Connolly, an outspoken critic of the US leader.
"I conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted," Connolly said in a post-meeting statement.
He then met Martin, when the Iran war and US tariffs on EU pharmaceuticals and immigration were on the agenda.
Ireland and the United States have long been close allies, partly because of their common ancestral ties.
But the Irish government's politics diverge sharply from those of the Trump administration on many issues, with Ireland being one of Europe's most pro-Palestinian countries.
Ireland is among several countries, including Spain, the UK and France, that have announced a trade ban targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
After a brief visit to the US embassy, Trump then flew to his Doonbeg resort - a remote, coastal site in County Clare that the Trump Organization purchased in 2014.
'Not welcome'
In Dublin, at least 2,000 protesters waving Palestinian flags and holding placards rallied against the visit, chanting "Donald Trump's not welcome here", according to AFP reporters.
One sign read "no imperialists in Ireland" while some held explicit inflatable balloons showing Trump in sex acts with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Trump is a warmonger," student Cillian Whelan, 19, told AFP. "He has no right to be in my country. He should be on trial."
Trump's attendance at the Irish Open adds an extra layer of complexity to a security effort that is reportedly costing Ireland 20 million euros ($23 million).
Some 40,000 fans are expected at the tournament over the weekend, with six-time major winner and current world number two Rory McIlroy the main draw.
The 80-year-old billionaire has promoted his family's golf business unabashedly since returning to the White House for his second stint as president in January 2025.
Last summer, he welcomed then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer and European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen to his plush resort at Turnberry on Scotland's west coast.
The golf-mad president may even award the trophy on Sunday.
"He's really just visiting the golf resort he owns and dropping into Dublin for a courtesy visit," Daniel Geary, a US history professor at Trinity College Dublin, told AFP.
"He sees little difference between his private interests and his role as president."

9f228d8d08f8675c: Nvidia spent a whopping $20 billion late last year to license Groq’s AI accelerator tech and hire away key members of its engineering team in an everything-but-the-kitchen-sink deal. The acquihire technically left Groq’s core inference-as-a-service business intact, but was clearly architected in such a way as to fly under regulators' radar. Only it didn’t. This week, The New York Times reported that the US Department of Justice had launched an antitrust probe into the deal. It’s hard to argue that Nvidia didn’t strip the startup for parts. It may not have been a merger in the traditional sense, but without its engineering staff, Groq may as well be Nvidia’s puppet at this point. Despite this, Nvidia contends the deal is a great American success story. “The Groq story is a prime example of the American system working as designed to promote innovation, reward entrepreneurs, and benefit consumers. The law is designed to encourage America's startup ecosystem and promote the fundamental rights of inventors and workers to pursue their dreams,” an Nvidia statement provided to El Reg and other media reads. Whether the acquihire of Groq actually harmed competition is another matter entirely. But, even if the Justice Department did force Nvidia to unwind the team, it’s probably too late. What exactly did Nvidia buy? Nvidia’s Groq acquihire bought it two key assets: mature silicon and the talent necessary to continue its development. Groq – which, by the way, is completely unrelated to Elon Musk’s Grok model series – made a name for itself using SRAM-heavy dataflow accelerators to speed up LLM inference to hundreds and now thousands of tokens a second, something that GPU-based systems from Nvidia had struggled to do on their own. But while faster than GPUs, the accelerators couldn’t achieve rapid throughput. Think of it this way: If Groq’s LPUs were the F1 cars, Nvidia’s GPUs were more like a city bus. But combine the two and you get something more akin to a sport pickup. At GTC in March, Nvidia unveiled its LPX racks, which are powered by 256 Groq-3 accelerators. As we understand it, they are really lightly modified versions of the startup’s existing Groq-2 chip designs, which makes sense, because three months is absurdly fast to tape out new silicon. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang promised Groq-3 combined with its Vera Rubin GPU racks would deliver optimal performance across the entire spectrum of inference workloads. But, as we’ve discussed at length now, disaggregated compute architectures are not unique to Groq. Nvidia rival Cerebras is building similar systems with AWS and AMD, SambaNova is working with Intel, and d-Matrix and its partners are combining its in-memory compute platform with Nvidia GPUs to the same end as Nvidia’s Vera Rubin-LPX rack combo. The damage, if any, has been done Deals of this sort that are engineered to avoid regulatory scrutiny should get it anyway, several US senators have argued. While Nvidia didn’t outright buy Groq on paper, it may as well have. However, the real question for the DOJ is whether the deal was harmful to competition, and given the competitive landscape, proving harm may be easier said than done. But even if the DOJ found reason to litigate and was successful in unwinding the deal — it certainly wouldn’t be the first time regulators had torpedoed an Nvidia deal — it probably wouldn’t change much. Before Nvidia and Groq announced their licensing deal, the GPU giant was already laying the foundations for an ecosystem with its networking business at its center. In late 2024, the company contributed its MGX rack designs to the Open Compute Project (OCP) making it possible for any chipmaker to put their chips in racks originally designed for Nvidia GPUs. Then in mid-2025, GPUzilla opened its high-speed interconnect tech — the secret sauce that makes six dozen GPUs behave as one — to the broader industry through a licensing scheme called NVLink Fusion. As we recently discussed, the combination of open racks and Nvidia networking effectively meant that any chipmaker licensing the tech could slot their designs directly into Nvidia’s racks. If the DOJ blocked the acquihire and unwound the deal, Nvidia might lose direct control of LPU development and any revenues from the sale of the chips, but it wouldn’t necessarily be the end of its Groq LPX racks. Groq would just join the growing number of Nvidia hardware partners designing around the company’s AI factory ecosystem. In fact, if anything, the acquihire ensures that even if regulators eventually derail the deal, there will be plenty of alternatives lined up and ready to fill the void. ®
c79e8d36e323f0a9: GEORGE TOWN: The family of missing Malaysian hiker Muhammad Muhaimin Azhad Noor Hadi, 27, has urged the Special Malaysia Disaster Assistance and Rescue Team (Smart) to continue the search and rescue (SAR) operation in Nepal.
The family said they were disappointed and frustrated after learning that the Smart team involved in the flood relief mission in Nepal was expected to return to Malaysia soon.

Muhaimin was reported to have been hiking in Langtang Valley with two friends, Muhammad Adib Haikal Awang Mansor, 27, and Muhammad Zaki Othman, 29, before they went missing during the Aug 26 disaster.
His father, Noor Hadi Mohd Hassan, 62, questioned the decision to withdraw the team, saying the reasons and details of the operation had not been clearly explained.
"We were shocked and disappointed by the decision because we do not know how the process took place, including how the assets were withdrawn.
"We also wonder whether no further action can be taken, such as searching the affected villages.

"Until now, we do not know how the search was conducted. They said efforts had been made, but we do not know how extensive the search was," he told reporters at his home in Taman Tun Sardon here today.

Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan previously said the Smart team deployed for the Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) mission in Nepal was expected to return to Malaysia today or tomorrow.
The 11-member team departed for Nepal on Sept 4 aboard a Royal Malaysian Air Force (RMAF) A400M aircraft.
Noor Hadi said the family and relatives were appealing for the search to continue.
"If they are still alive, Alhamdulillah. But if not, we still want certainty. We hope the government will take this seriously and find the best way to resolve the situation.

"My health has deteriorated since the incident because I am worried and constantly thinking about my son. He has also been the one helping me with my movements," said Noor Hadi, who uses a wheelchair after losing one leg.
Muhaimin's mother, Zaleha Ariffin, 57, said she would accept whatever fate had been determined for her son but wanted a clear conclusion so the family would not be left waiting indefinitely.
"He is still young. He had told us several times that he wanted to get engaged and marry his chosen partner next year.

"He should be counting down the days to his happy occasion, but this is what has happened. We are deeply worried. I sincerely hope the authorities will make every effort to find him and bring him home," she said.
Meanwhile, Muhaimin's girlfriend, who declined to be named, said their last WhatsApp conversation was at 11am Malaysian time, about five minutes before the incident occurred at 8.45am Nepal time.
"He told me he had eaten chapati that day before contact was lost. I thought he had entered a forested area.
"Not long after that, I saw news of the incident on social media and informed Muhammad Muhaimin's family," she said.
baafeb93fedb2eb6: KULIM: Kementerian Dalam Negeri (KDN) bakal mengumumkan tarikh kuat kuasa pindaan peruntukan kewarganegaraan bagi anak yang dilahirkan di luar negara oleh wanita warga Malaysia, selepas semua persiapan selesai.

Menteri Dalam Negeri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail berkata penetapan tarikh kuat kuasa telah ditentukan oleh Yang di-Pertuan Agong dan KDN akan mengumumkannya selepas beberapa perkara membabitkan urusan pentadbiran selesai.

"Persiapan turut melibatkan penyediaan sistem permohonan dalam talian kerana pelaksanaannya akan membabitkan pejabat perwakilan Malaysia di seluruh negara," katanya kepada pemberita pada program bersama menteri.

Beliau berkata empat kategori utama yang merekodkan jumlah permohonan tinggi ialah di bawah Perkara 15A, Perkara 15(2), Perkara 19(1) dan Perkara 30(1) Perlembagaan Persekutuan.

0e69ef08543b4f86: PETALING JAYA: The G25 group of prominent retired civil servants has warned that a proposal by PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang to remove "colonial-era laws" — which he said hinder shariah law implementation — would pave the way for establishing a theocracy in Malaysia.
G25 said Hadi's proposal would place one interpretation of Islamic law above the Federal Constitution, and "place a small group of clerics above the rulers, above Parliament and above the courts".
"That is a theocracy, and the founders of this country, Malay and Muslim as they were, rejected it," said the group in a statement.

G25 rejected Hadi's call for the Civil Law Act 1956 to be abolished so that the country would no longer be “fully bound” by English common law, and for a constitutional amendment stating that any law that conflicted with Islamic teachings would be rejected.

G25 said the Civil Law Act was carried into independence by Malaysia's founding fathers, who chose a working legal system. "To call these laws colonial is an attempt to play politics with the foundation of this country," the group said.

G25 said the Federal Constitution is a covenant that Malaysians of every faith have honoured for nearly 70 years. Honouring covenants is itself an Islamic obligation, the group said, pointing out that the constitution already gives Islam its place as the federation's official religion, makes the rulers heads of the religion in their states and also protects Muslims.

On Sept 9, Hadi called for the abolition of all colonial-era laws, especially those that prevent Islam from taking precedence over “man-made laws that are not permitted by Allah because of their many shortcomings that spread sinfulness”.

G25 said Muslims believe that God's law is perfect. However, what human authorities apply is "fiqh", the interpretation of learned men, which differs between schools of thought and, in Malaysia, between 14 enactments across the 13 states and the federal territories.
Hadi had taken aim at the Syariah Courts (Criminal Jurisdiction) Act 1965 which he said prevented the imposition of heavier shariah criminal punishments.

G25 rejected Hadi's claim that the laws were colonial. It said Parliament had enacted the Shariah Courts Act in 1965, while the Civil Law Act, was carried into independence by Malaysia's founding fathers.

"It applies the common law only where Malaysian written law is silent and only so far as local circumstances permit, and Parliament can displace it by ordinary legislation at any time, as it has done previously," added the group.

G25 also warns that repealing this Act would remove the basis on which the courts apply the common law and the rules of equity that underpin tort, trusts, commercial dealings and every area where Parliament has not legislated in full.

"The legal uncertainty and cost to investor confidence would be unprecedented. Malaysia's Islamic finance industry, among the largest in the world, is built on federal statutes and enforced in the civil courts, and undermining that framework would harm the very Muslim institutions the PAS president says he wishes to strengthen," G25 said.

492b00c727b91f3c: HONG KONG, Sept 12 — China and Nepal have taken different approaches to information after a Himalayan flood, shaping what the public saw of a disaster that killed more than 1,400 people.
The August 26 tsunami-like surge of water, mud and debris from a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border left more than 5,650 missing, including hundreds of foreigners.
Both China and Nepal have gone after fabricated posts on the flood.
But Beijing has gone further to suppress eyewitness video footage and punish people challenging official figures, in an information crackdown that rights groups say follows a familiar pattern.

Information transmitted by Chinese state media on the flood gave little voice to the missing people’s relatives and focused on emergency workers’ recovery efforts in Tibet, where foreign journalists do not enjoy unfettered access.

Nepal has pressured social media platforms and news outlets to remove fabricated visuals — including some debunked by AFP fact-checkers — but Kathmandu offers regular updates of death tolls via social media. Direct commentary from families of victims is readily available on and offline.
Umesh Shrestha, chair of the independent regulatory body Press Council Nepal, said it had asked more than 100 social media accounts to remove content. Most obeyed.
“Things can spread very quickly,” Shrestha said.
Nepali police arrested one man who allegedly shared a fabricated donation to a relief fund to promote his personal account.
The disaster came just ahead of the one-year anniversary of anti-corruption protests that toppled the previous government, triggered by a social media ban.
China penalised 10 people accused of spreading falsehoods online, according to the Ministry of Public Security.
They include some who allegedly suggested the actual death toll was higher than official figures.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Offerings placed by workers to mourn the victims of the August 26 mudslide are seen at the site of the destroyed Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, in China’s western Tibet region on September 5, 2026. — CNS/China OUT/AFP pic
Beijing’s foreign ministry insists the release of information has been “open, transparent and timely”, and criticised what it has called “malicious smearing and sensationalism”.
It also organised a trip for a small number of foreign media to the Tibetan epicentre of the disaster.
‘Public panic’
AFP fact-checkers have debunked dozens of claims about the floods in multiple languages.
One video that falsely claimed to show the glacial and mountain collapse that caused the flooding – posted on Facebook and X – was filmed in Alaska’s Columbia Glacier days beforehand.
Other footage created using Google’s AI tools showed water breaching a riverbank and flooding streets and amassed tens of thousands of interactions.
“During disasters, public panic is high,” said Nepali investigative journalist Rabi Raj Baral, who is also a member of the Press Council Nepal.
But both Nepal and China have not only gone after fabrications, but have also targeted posts including some sharing genuine footage.
Nepali authorities have held talks with Meta and TikTok to speed up the removal of AI content, graphic images and fraudulent aid schemes.
Both platforms pay AFP to fact-check posts with potentially false information.
Video verified by AFP as showing the deluge engulfing Gyirong Port – the border post with Nepal – and other eyewitness content have largely disappeared from the Chinese internet.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Repair work has been paused along a road leading to Gyirong Port after a mudslide damaged it in Gyirong County, western Tibet, on August 28, 2026, amid the threat of new flooding. — AFP pic
Social media sites such as Douyin and Weibo have instead featured extensive state media coverage of search operations, without naming the missing or showing much footage of families’ reactions.
‘Atmosphere of mistrust’
AFP fact-checkers found flood-related misinformation is mostly absent from Chinese platforms, although conspiracy theories have blossomed abroad.

Posts shared from Canada to South Korea allege China lied about the death toll, and that its dam construction projects caused the disaster — even though scientists say a glacial collapse in Nepal was to blame.
Online critics also point to the fact that the vast bulk of the dead and missing reported by the two governments are in Nepal.

In Nepal, rescuers have retrieved 1,369 bodies, while around 5,132 people are missing, according to the disaster agency Thursday. In China, the toll is 43 dead and 519 missing, according to state media.
The stark difference, however, may be a reflection of the disaster’s geography and scale.

The glacial mountain collapse occurred in downstream Nepal, sending a wave of debris so powerful it smashed China’s high-altitude border post in tightly restricted Tibet, before carving a path of destruction across Nepal.
Bodies on the Chinese side may have washed downstream too, but because of the geography, they could be buried in a thick layer of mud and debris that makes recovery impossible.
Aleksandra Bielakowska, a Taipei-based advocacy manager for Reporters Without Borders (RSF), said that Beijing’s restrictions had created an “atmosphere of mistrust”.
In contrast, Celia Mercier, head of RSF’s South Asia Desk, said Nepal had “largely treated misinformation as a problem within an otherwise relatively open information environment”. — AFP
ec6ddd48118d7177: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 12 — Rain and heavy traffic did little to dampen the warm atmosphere inside Barra Restaurant on Wednesday, where Spanish diplomats, chefs, and food lovers gathered to celebrate a shared appreciation for good food.
For Spain’s Ambassador-designate to Malaysia Sergi Farré Salvá, food offers a natural connection between Spain and Malaysia, a country where eating is deeply woven into everyday life.

“One of the first words that we learn when we come here in Bahasa Melayu is makan,” said Farré, who arrived in Malaysia a month ago. “So, we are going to do lots of makan-makan today,” he added, drawing laughter from the guests.
Farré called food a “universal connector” and described his first dining experience at Barra as more than simply a meal.
“It was a cultural experience, an artistic experience,” he said, highlighting the combination of tradition, creativity, and innovation that characterises Spanish gastronomy.
The ambassador-designate is expected to present his credentials to His Majesty Sultan Ibrahim, King of Malaysia, in late October or early November this year.
During the event, Farré officially presented the Restaurants From Spain certification plaque to Chef Gabriel Bonin, Chef Ignasi Prats, and the Barra team.

Awarded by the Spanish government through ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the certification recognises restaurants outside Spain that offer authentic, high-quality Spanish cuisine and promote Spanish culinary products and culture.
Farré said the certification was reserved for outstanding establishments and Barra’s inclusion had brought the number of certified Spanish restaurants in Kuala Lumpur to eight.
“That says a lot about Malaysia and what this capital stands for. Food happens 24 hours a day, seven days a week here. It is a paradise for any food lover,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A selection of authentic Spanish dishes served to guests during the Restaurants From Spain certification ceremony at Barra Restaurant here on September 9. — Bernama pic
He also stressed that Spain’s culinary reputation was built not only on its centuries-old heritage and the influence of civilisations across the Mediterranean, but also on continuous innovation.
“You cannot have this level of gastronomy without innovation, science, and technology that cooks and chefs like Gabriel and Ignasi bring,” he said.

The Embassy of Spain in Malaysia’s Chief Economic and Commercial Counsellor Juan Guía said the gathering served two objectives: to celebrate Barra’s certification and formally introduce the second edition of the Eat Spain Drink Spain festival in Malaysia.
He said the campaign sought to make Spanish food more accessible to Malaysians while encouraging people to discover it together with their families and friends.
“Spanish gastronomy is known globally for its creativity and diversity, and for being deeply rooted in our history and heritage.
“Eat Spain Drink Spain is about bringing our gastronomy to Malaysia for locals to enjoy and discover with their friends and families,” he said.
The festival, scheduled from Sept 18 to Oct 4, will take place in more than 40 participating venues across Malaysia, including Kuala Lumpur, Melaka, Johor, Penang, and Kuching.

The embassy’s foreign trade and investment official Andrea Lázaro said participating establishments would offer a variety of experiences, including two-week promotional menus, weekend pop-ups, and one-day tapas events.
Some venues will highlight traditional favourites such as paella, tortilla de patatas, and Basque cheesecake, while others will present more contemporary interpretations of Spanish cuisine.

Lázaro clarified that Eat Spain Drink Spain is a separate initiative from the Restaurants From Spain certification. Eat Spain Drink Spain is an annual international festival organised by ICEX in which restaurants and other venues host their own Spanish food and beverage events.
Barra, which opened in April 2024, is a restaurant under The Tamarind Restaurants group which Guía described as a “piece of Barcelona” in one of Kuala Lumpur’s Chinese neighbourhoods.
The group’s restaurants and dining concepts in the Kuala Lumpur area were founded and conceptualised by Federico Asaro, chief executive officer and driving force behind Samadhi Retreats.
Guía also credited Prats and Bonin for building Barra’s identity.
Bonin said the certification carried both pride and responsibility for the restaurant’s team.

“We are really proud to be part of the Spanish community, to show Spain to the world and to show our gastronomy,” he said. “It is a big challenge for us, but at the same time, receiving this recognition keeps us giving our best.”
22f35cffe86ef569: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 12 — News consumption has reached a turning point: social media now edges television and news websites as the most widely used source of news.
This changing mix of traditional and digital news sources is reflected in the 2026 edition of the annual Digital News Report, published by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism.
Across the 48 markets covered in 2026, social media was the most widely used source of news, averaging 54 per cent. Television followed at 52 per cent, while news websites were used by 51 per cent.

In 2017, television led at 73 per cent and news websites at 69 per cent, while social media stood at 54 per cent. Its move into first place therefore reflects the decline of the other two sources more than long-term growth in its own reach.
Social media dominates Malaysia’s news mix
Malaysia’s shift is even more pronounced. Nearly seven in 10 respondents used social media for news in 2026, compared with 42 per cent for news websites and 36 per cent for television.
What stands out over the decade is not the growth of social media, which has remained above 60 per cent since 2017, but the retreat of established news channels.
News website use fell 24 per centage points and television dropped 18 points. Print recorded the steepest fall at 31 points.
Radio remained a smaller and more volatile source, reaching 23 per cent in 2026.

Among Malaysian respondents overall, AI chatbot use stood at 11 per cent in 2026, compared with nine per cent in 2025. Podcast use was eight percent, compared with nine percent the year before. With only two years of data available for both, it is too early to establish a longer-term direction.
Social media is not only where Malaysians consume news. Increasingly, it is how they find it.
In 2026, 63 per cent discovered news through social media, compared with 44 per cent through search engines and just 27 per cent through direct visits to news websites and apps.
Other routes remained less common, with news aggregators and mobile alerts both at 20 per cent, while email stood at 12 per cent.

Taken together, the figures suggest that the change is not simply a move from traditional to digital media. Social media now plays a dual role: it is both a source of news and the main route through which Malaysians discover it.
WhatsApp and video platforms gain ground
The platforms carrying that news are changing too.
WhatsApp overtook Facebook as Malaysia’s most widely used platform for news in 2026, although only narrowly, at 50 per cent versus 49 per cent.
The bigger shift, however, has been towards video. TikTok surged from just two per cent in 2019 to 45 per cent in 2026, while YouTube climbed from 26 per cent to 41 per cent over the decade.
Together, their growth points to video becoming a much larger part of how Malaysians find, watch and share news.

The platform mix also continues to change. Threads reached 11 per cent in 2026 after appearing in the survey at two per cent in 2024, while X fell to nine percent after peaking at 22 per cent in 2022.
That growing dependence on social platforms also raises a harder question: how carefully are users checking what reaches them?

The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission’s Internet Users Survey 2024 found that 61.5 per cent of internet users shared news, while the proportion checking its validity and source reliability fell from 79.2 per cent to 70.7 per cent.

The survey also noted growing reliance on automated or platform-based fact-checking. It added that trust in online content was declining amid the rise of fake news, particularly political and health misinformation.
News habits differ by age and gender
Social media crossed generations, with usage ranging from 65 to 71 per cent across every age group in 2026.

The sharper differences appeared in the use of other news sources. Respondents aged 55 and above recorded higher use of news websites, television, radio and print than younger age groups, while younger Malaysians were more likely to turn to newer formats.
That contrast was especially clear with AI chatbots. Twenty-one per cent who use them in 2026 were among those aged 18 to 24. A mere six per cent of the respondents were aged 45 and above.
Podcast use showed a similar, though less pronounced, pattern, with younger respondents recording the highest use.

The age divide was therefore not a simple split between digital and traditional media. Older Malaysians remained active on social media while continuing to use established news sources at higher rates, whereas younger users were more likely to add newer formats such as AI chatbots and podcasts to their news habits.

A study of Malaysian Generation Z published in Media Asia identified virality, news awareness, the ubiquity of news and credibility as themes in how participants understood news. The findings offer some context for a media environment in which news appears alongside entertainment, personal updates and commentary rather than occupying a space of its own.
Gender differences were modest for social media but considerably wider for some established news sources.

Social media use was almost identical among women and men, at 69 and 68 per cent respectively. News websites showed the biggest gap, however, reaching 48 per cent of men compared with 36 percent of women.

The pattern was less pronounced for AI chatbots. In 2026, they were used for news by 12 perc ent of men and 11 per cent of women, after use among women rose from seven per cent the previous year. Podcast use showed a wider difference, at 10 per cent among men and six per cent among women.

For Malaysians, the shift today is not simply about where news is consumed, but how it is discovered, shared and encountered. Traditional sources remain important, especially among older audiences, but social platforms now play a much greater role in determining what news reaches people in the first place.
Note on the data:

The Digital News Report is based on annual online surveys conducted by YouGov. For the 2026 edition, fieldwork was carried out between mid-January and the end of February. The Malaysian sample comprised 2,076 respondents, while annual samples from 2017 to 2026 ranged from 2,004 to 2,108 respondents.

The number of markets covered increased from 36 in 2017 to 48 in 2025 and 2026, meaning the international trend figures are annual averages across the markets surveyed rather than a fixed group. Respondents could select more than one news source, so the figures do not add up to 100 per cent or represent market shares. — Bernama
21fe40a1ed4f3431: SAN FRANCISCO, Sept 12 — ChatGPT maker OpenAI confirmed today that autonomous software built on its models targeted another website during testing a couple of months before a separate attack on the coding site Hugging Face.
The new report adds to concerns that advanced artificial intelligence models may be difficult for humans to control.

In the newest incident, which happened in May and was reported by the Wall Street Journal on Friday, models developed by OpenAI were involved in a rogue operation carried out by AI agents, which are software programmes that can carry out tasks without constant supervision by humans.
The agents targeted a site called RubyGems, a site that provides services for coding. Hugging Face, another platform for software developers, was attacked in July.
“Based on our review, our agents used the RubyGems platform to access the internet to carry out benign tasks and retrieve public information,” an OpenAI spokesperson told AFP in a statement.
“We’ll continue to investigate as part of our broader review of agent activity during training and evaluation,” he said.
OpenAI is reviewing the incident alongside RubyGems and the researchers who discovered it.
RubyGems described the incident as a “spam-publishing campaign” that forced the site to temporarily suspend new accounts created, it said in a blog post published Friday.
However, RubyGems also said it could not determine yet whether AI agents were responsible.
“Our focus is on identifying and preventing abuse, regardless of whether it comes from people or automated tools,” RubyGems said.
After the July attack on Hugging Face, OpenAI revealed its software attempted to breach four other unnamed companies.

Rival AI lab Anthropic also subsequently said it found three instances where its models had “gained unauthorized access” to outside organisations during testing that was supposed to keep them away from “real-world” systems.
Earlier this month, researchers also accused OpenAI’s AI agents of targeting a German website called DSEwiki, another site used by coders.
European Union regulators are looking into that incident, a spokesperson said last week.
“We have seen many losses of control recently. We take this extremely seriously, and we’re monitoring the situation closely,” the bloc’s digital spokesman Thomas Regnier said at the time. — AFP

9d57fbf8d252a330: FIRST LOOK Dell's UltraSharp 52 display is a joyously enormous head-turner, but probably too much monitor for most users. Dell debuted the display at the CES show earlier this year. It's now on sale for $3,000. Sadly, I lack a PC capable of driving the screen at its full 6144 x 2560 resolution and 120 Hz refresh rate. Even at a miserly 3840 x 2160, however, I often marveled at how much it could display. Consider the screenshot below, which shows 50 columns and 89 rows of a single Excel spreadsheet – 4,450 cells in total. Here's another look at the monitor in full flight: a screen grab of Zwift, the virtual cycling metaverse I visit regularly as part of my exercise routine. At that size, Zwift felt more immersive and enjoyable than it does on a smaller screen. The display also handled motion smoothly during Zwift. other games, and streamed video. Getting used to it It took me a while to appreciate the monitor. When I first plugged it in, my occasionally-stiff middle-aged neck strained as I swiveled to view content at the edges and corners, while wielding my mouse to move its pointer between the screen's extremities felt like flapping my arms. My eyes didn't enjoy the experience at first either. I wear mild reading glasses while working, and found myself repeatedly refocusing as I looked across the curved display. For the first few days I spent with the screen, I therefore practiced "pillarboxing" – running the display at 3840 x 2160 and only using the center of the monitor while pixels on the edges remained dark. That didn't feel odd or distracting, perhaps because I often use "letterboxing" while watching video on my TV or tablet – leaving pixels at the top and bottom of the screen unused. As I grew accustomed to the enormo-monitor, I began using its entire area. Getting there was not straightforward: each of the three PCs I used with the monitor (one at a time, not together) required manual adjustment before I found a resolution that did not distort text and images. Dell's companion app was no help. It was slow to install, ran as if stuck in digital treacle, and is little more than a glorified front end for the Windows System/Display control panel. The HDMI connection to my desktop – an Acemagic mini-PC – repeatedly dropped out, forcing me to reseat the cable every day. The same PC and cable work reliably with my everyday monitor. I tried another cable and the problem persisted. I reached out to Dell, who suggested my two different cables were to blame. I connected my laptop – a Dell Inspiron Plus 7441 – over Thunderbolt and experienced some flickering that went away without needing to reseat the cable. A ten-year-old ThinkPad Carbon X1 connected fine over HDMI, but had even more trouble finding appropriate settings. But once I got the machine going and got used to its colossal size, my initial fatigue vanished. I realized I was squinting a little less than I do with my everyday display, a seven-year-old 32-inch Samsung that lacks the HDR feature the Dell machine includes. I sometimes use my lunch breaks to watch some rugby highlights, and the display handled those with ease. The easily observable nuances of small ads on team shirts would doubtless please sponsors. I was also pleasantly surprised by the display's speakers, which rendered my favorite tunes brightly and crisply. My current high rotation tunes include guitar feedback legends The Jesus and Mary Chain, spiky garage pop from Welsh outfit The Bug Club, and mumbly "power disco" by Getdown Services. JAMC's trademark fuzz was warm and deep, I felt like I could hear new strings on The Bug Club's guitars, and Getdown Services' beats thumped meatily. The speakers' location at the rear of the monitor led to a few "Where's that sound coming from?" moments, but those quickly became tolerable. Weighty issues I was impressed by Dell's packaging, which places the cables and included stand in clearly marked cardboard compartments within the shell protecting the screen. That matters because the box is a whopper that would be difficult to lug out of an IKEA and into a small car. Easy access to the assembly parts means a little less wrestling. At 12.95 kg (28.5 lbs), the monitor isn't problematically heavy – but is maybe too weighty for Dell's stand, as it never sat perfectly level, and I could find no way to straighten it. The screen is also unwieldy: I recommend connecting any cables you plan to use in advance, because shifting and lifting it to access its ports is not easy, especially in constricted spaces behind a desk. Tucked under the monitor's bottom-left edge is a forward-facing USB hub with two USB-C ports and one USB-A port. Making one of them a Thunderbolt port would have made it easier to connect a laptop without rummaging behind the beast. I finished my time with this giant display convinced that it is a lovely machine, but not one I need, as my work consists mostly of writing and editing text and browsing the web. Those who work with visual material may adore its size and the immersion created by its gentle curve. Many of Dell's promotional images show the device displaying multiple financial data feeds. The company pitches it as a replacement for four smaller monitors, requiring only one power cable and dispensing with a complex collection of stands. That seems like a more sensible use of the screen than everyday knowledge work. To finish, here's one more photo. I started working from home in 2002 but had no room to dedicate to an office. I therefore splurged about $700 – big bucks at the time – on a 15-inch, 1024 x 768 Dell 1503FP LCD monitor so that a CRT did not dominate my lounge room. It still works, although when the time came to take this snap, I couldn't find the HDMI-to-VGA adapter I use to fire it up. Here it is anyway, posed in front of its giant descendant to offer some historical perspective on how monitors have grown. ®
